page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.g6.xlarge is a general-purpose virtual machine instance powered by the KVM hypervisor. It features 4 dedicated vCPUs based on the x86_64 architecture, utilizing an Intel Xeon 8269CY processor running at a clock speed of 2.5 GHz. The hardware configuration includes 4 physical cores with 1.0 thread per core, 16.0 GB of system memory (providing 4.0 GB per core), and a baseline network bandwidth of 2 Gbps. This instance does not include local storage or GPU accelerators. The CPU is equipped with 32 KB of L1d cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 35 MB of L3 cache, supporting instruction sets such as AVX, AVX-512, and AES cryptography.

Benchmark evaluations place the performance of the ecs.g6.xlarge mostly in the lower tiers. In CPU-intensive tasks, the instance achieved a stress-ng single-core score of 1305.28 and a multi-core score of 3458.1, both falling within the bottom 25% of tested hardware. Geekbench testing yielded an average single-core score of 1156.0, while the multi-core score of 2546.0 was categorized as weak. Memory performance is mixed, with a PassMark memory score of 1902.06 reaching average levels, though large-block read and write bandwidths remained low at 25.47 GB/sec and 22.43 GB/sec respectively. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression registered a poor result of 16.96 GB/sec, placing it in the bottom 10%.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the ecs.g6.xlarge offers a standard general-purpose resource density with its 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, though its benchmark-per-resource return is constrained by its older Intel Xeon processor generation. The lack of bundled local storage requires users to attach external block storage, which introduces additional architectural considerations. Given the weak multi-core processing and database benchmark results (such as 1384.85 in PassMark database operations and 3.37 million operations/sec in Redis SET), this instance is appropriate for lightweight general-purpose workloads, basic web serving, development environments, and low-intensity background tasks rather than high-throughput database or heavy computational workloads.
